planting.note: Set out rooted offsets in spring once soil has warmed, in a site with sharp drainage.

directions: A striking sport of Agave americana var. striata, with long gray-glaucous leaves running a broad, sharply defined central band of buttery yellow rather than the marginal cream stripe seen on 'Marginata' or 'Variegata'. Leaf margins carry small recurved teeth and a stout terminal spine, so keep it away from paths. Grow in full sun with fast-draining, lean soil and minimal supplemental water once established; like most large century plants it is monocarpic, flowering once on a towering stalk after many years before the rosette dies, leaving offsets to carry on. Cold hardy into the mid-teens Fahrenheit, making it usable well beyond the mildest zones.

planting.note: Give it a permanent, wide-open site in spring — this is one of the largest agaves grown and resents being moved once established.

directions: An enormous, open rosette of thick, arching gray-green leaves six to nine feet long with only minimal marginal teeth and a heavy dark terminal spine — among the largest agaves cultivated, dwarfing even Agave americana at maturity. This variegated selection traces to tissue-cultured material from a Huntington Botanic Gardens specimen and rarely offsets, so plants are propagated almost entirely by micropropagation rather than division. Plant it only where its eventual nine-foot-plus spread and towering, multi-story flower spike can be accommodated; give it full sun, sharp drainage, and very little supplemental irrigation once rooted in. Historically the species was tapped for pulque production in central Mexico, distinguishing it culturally from purely ornamental agaves.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings and plant out after frost danger has passed.

directions: Forms tidy, uniform rosettes to about six inches across on branching stems, with dark purple-black upper leaf faces set off by noticeably paler undersides and fresh green new growth at the rosette center — a two-tone effect that is more pronounced than on the taller, larger-rosetted 'Zwartkop'. Rosettes hold their form and leaf count after flowering rather than collapsing, and yellow flowers are borne low within the clump in summer instead of terminally. Give it full coastal sun or light afternoon shade inland, with lean, fast-draining soil and only occasional water; it is markedly more cold-tender than hardy Aeonium species and should be moved under cover below the high 20s Fahrenheit.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings in spring in bright, cool-sun exposure.

directions: A tall, shrubby Tenerife endemic that builds a branched woody framework to four to six feet, each stem topped by a large terminal rosette of gray-green leaves edged with fine reddish cilia, with smaller secondary rosettes breaking along the stem below. It is separated from the similar Aeonium urbicum by its hairless (glabrous) leaf surfaces and consistently branching habit, versus urbicum's hairy leaves on mostly solitary rosettes, and it blooms later, in early summer, with dome-shaped clusters of cream flowers rather than spring. More sun intensifies the red leaf-margin color and keeps growth compact; shadier siting produces taller, greener plants. Wants a cool-summer coastal climate with occasional irrigation and sharp drainage, and is not reliably hardy below the mid-to-upper 20s Fahrenheit.

planting.note: Set out rooted offsets in spring; give it cool-sun to light-shade exposure.

directions: A hybrid likely tracing to Aeonium canariense, forming broad flattened green rosettes that offset freely into a dense mounding colony rather than growing on tall single stems. Pale yellow to cream flower clusters appear on short stalks in early summer; flowering rosettes die back afterward but are quickly hidden by the surrounding non-flowering growth, so the clump stays full-looking year-round. Site it in cool coastal sun or light shade with lean, sharply drained soil and infrequent water — it tolerates salt spray and is generally left alone by deer, but is tender and should be protected below the high 20s Fahrenheit.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings and plant out in spring in cool sun to light shade.

directions: Sometimes labeled Aeonium undulatum ssp. pseudotabuliforme, this uncommon Canary Island hybrid produces flattened rosettes six to ten inches across of glossy, rounded green leaves held tightly on a low, laterally branching stem to about a foot or two tall. Unlike the true dinner-plate aeonium (A. tabuliforme), which sits nearly flat on the ground as a single unbranched rosette, this one builds a shrubby, multi-headed mound over time and is far easier to propagate from cut stems. A pyramidal cluster of yellow flowers rises from mature rosettes in spring. Best in cool-summer coastal sun to part shade with summer-dry, well-drained conditions and only moderate water; useful as a groundcover, container specimen, or textural front-of-border accent.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings and set out in spring once nights stay above the low 40s.

directions: A chance seedling that arose near Aeonium arboreum 'Zwartkop' at a California nursery, notable for large undulating rosettes whose new leaves emerge fresh green at the base and darken quickly to a rich red-purple toward the tips, giving each rosette a two-tone green-centered, red-rimmed look distinct from the uniformly near-black 'Zwartkop'. Bears yellow flower clusters in summer on branching stems reaching two to three feet. Best color develops in full coastal sun or bright part shade inland, with lean, fast-draining soil and minimal irrigation once established; tolerates seaside exposure but is tender and needs frost protection below the high 20s Fahrenheit.
